title: Binary Search Variants — First/Last Occurrence & Rotated Arrays
summary: The same halving invariant, aimed at trickier targets — finding the first or last of a run of duplicates, and searching a rotated sorted array by identifying which half is still properly ordered.

slides.markdown:
[binary-search-fundamentals](binary-search-fundamentals) established the invariant that makes binary search correct. This topic applies that same invariant to two problem shapes that trip candidates up specifically because the target isn't a single clean value: finding the **first or last** occurrence among duplicates, and searching a **rotated** sorted array where the array isn't globally sorted anymore, just sorted in two pieces.

Both are still genuinely O(log n) — the trick in each case is identifying what property of the array *is* still monotonic (still increases predictably) even though the naive "is it sorted" check fails.

slides.sectionTitle: Finding the first occurrence among duplicates
slides.markdown:
Given a sorted array with duplicates, find the **first** index where the target appears. A naive binary search that returns on the first `arr[mid] == target` gives you *some* matching index, but not necessarily the first one.

The fix: when `arr[mid] == target`, don't stop — record `mid` as a candidate answer, then keep searching the **left** half (`hi = mid - 1`) for an even earlier occurrence. This is exactly `lower_bound`'s logic in different framing: keep narrowing toward the boundary even after finding a match, because a match doesn't mean you've found the *first* match.

The mirror image: find the **last** index where the target appears. Same idea, opposite direction — when `arr[mid] == target`, record `mid` as a candidate and keep searching the **right** half (`lo = mid + 1`) for an even later occurrence, rather than stopping or narrowing left.

Both first and last occurrence share the same core discipline: a match is never immediately a final answer, it's a candidate that might be improved by continuing to search in one specific direction.

A rotated sorted array (e.g., `[4,5,6,7,0,1,2]` — the sorted array `[0,1,2,4,5,6,7]` rotated so it starts partway through) isn't globally sorted anymore, so plain binary search's "is target bigger or smaller than mid" comparison doesn't directly apply.

The key insight that rescues binary search: **at least one of the two halves, split at any midpoint, is always properly sorted.** Check which half is sorted (compare `arr[lo]` to `arr[mid]`), then check whether the target falls within that sorted half's range — if it does, recurse there; if not, it must be in the other half.

The picture should make the recognition step concrete: whichever half contains no "drop" (no point where a later element is smaller than an earlier one) is the properly sorted half, and comparing just the endpoints (`arr[lo]` vs `arr[mid]`) is enough to tell which one that is without scanning either half.

slides.sectionTitle: Finding the rotation point as its own search
slides.markdown:
The rotation point (the index of the minimum element, where the "break" in sorted order happens) can be found with its own binary search, independent of any target value: compare `arr[mid]` to `arr[hi]`. If `arr[mid] > arr[hi]`, the minimum must be somewhere to the right of `mid` (the break hasn't happened yet); if `arr[mid] <= arr[hi]`, the minimum is at `mid` or to its left (the right portion is already the sorted, un-rotated tail).

This is a useful building block on its own — some problems ask for the rotation count directly, and it's also a clean way to convert a rotated-array search into two plain binary searches (find the pivot, then binary search the correct one of the two resulting sorted sub-arrays) if the combined single-pass version feels harder to get right under pressure.

With duplicates allowed (e.g., `[2,2,2,0,2,2]`), the "which half is sorted" check can become ambiguous: if `arr[lo] == arr[mid] == arr[hi]`, you genuinely cannot tell which half contains the rotation point from that comparison alone — both halves *look* uniform.

The fix costs the algorithm's guarantee: when this ambiguous case is hit, shrink the window by one from either side (`lo += 1; hi -= 1`) and try again, rather than being able to confidently discard half the array. This makes the worst case (all duplicates) degrade to O(n) — a real, provable cost, not just a theoretical footnote — since no shortcut exists when every element looks identical to the pivot-detection check.

slides.sectionTitle: Rotated-array search vs plain binary search
slides.markdown:
| | Plain binary search | Rotated-array search |
|---|---|---|
| Extra step per iteration | None | Determine which half is currently sorted |
| Comparison basis | `arr[mid]` vs `target` directly | `arr[lo]` vs `arr[mid]` first, then target against the sorted half's range |
| Worst case (no duplicates) | O(log n) | O(log n) |
| Worst case (with duplicates, ambiguous case) | O(log n) unaffected | Degrades to O(n) |

The algorithm is still fundamentally "halve the search space" — the added complexity is entirely in correctly identifying *which* half is the reliably-sorted one before applying the usual target-range logic.

slides.sectionTitle: Assuming the left half is always sorted
slides.markdown:
A common mistake: hard-coding the assumption that the left half is always the sorted one, and only ever checking the right half's range against the target. On a rotation where the **right** half happens to be the sorted one (which half is sorted depends entirely on where the rotation point falls relative to `mid`, and flips depending on the specific rotation), this silently gives wrong answers on roughly half of all possible rotation points, while appearing to work on the other half.

The correct approach always checks explicitly (`arr[lo] <= arr[mid]`) rather than assuming — the sorted half genuinely alternates between left and right depending on where the rotation point sits relative to the current search window, and skipping that check is a bug that specific test inputs can easily fail to expose.
